newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Britain's Blair storms into Europe.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Blair storms into Europe.

text.p: European leaders were expecting things to be different after Tony Blair's landslide election victory. Things were different, but not quite as expected.
Eurosceptic Conservatives had given apocalyptic warnings during the campaign that Britain's new Labour Prime Minister would hand over sovereignty to Europe.
The mood was certainly different at a one-day meeting of European Union leaders called to get to know the new British leader.
"There are good things (in Europe), let us celebrate them," Blair told a news conference after the meeting in this Dutch coastal resort.
But behind the warm words was the glint of steely determination which has taken even enthusiasts at home by surprise.

In Britain, Blair has stunned people lulled into a false sense of security by charges his election manifesto contained little new. In his first three weeks in power he has hit the ground running with radical changes to the Bank of England and to financial market regulation.
In Europe, Blair's first formal speech to his fellow EU leaders was a stern warning that they were out of touch with voters and missing the point.
Instead of fussing about internal reform and EU institutions, Europe's elite had to start worrying about the things on the mind of average citizens -- their jobs and the environment.
"We want measures that deal with the problems that the citizens of Europe face...on jobs, on crime, on the problems of the environment, on consumer rights," said Blair.
The "visceral anti-Europeanism" of the eurosceptics who dogged ousted prime minister John Major's dying days was over, promised Blair.
But just in case anyone thought that made him a pushover, Blair laid out his bottom line.
"Britain's right to determine its own defence, immmigration policies and taxation policies...is sacrosanct and absolute," Blair said.

Britain's Labour government would end the opt-out negotiated by Major and sign up for the social chapter -- designed to set common levels of protection for workers across the bloc -- in a sign of its new constructive approach.
But it would not allow the chapter to be used to usher in an avalanche of proposals which would hinder the creation of jobs.
The language sounded eerily familiar.

If, just a few weeks earlier, Major -- whose Conservative government had slashed through union legislation and created Britain's flexible labour market -- had used the same language, the headlines would have been along the lines of "Battling Major lays down law in Europe".
But what was the headline in London's Evening Standard -- a late convert to Blair on the eve of the election? "New Labour, new Europe".
The reaction from Blair's fellow leaders, expecting a new constructive approach after 18 years of Conservative rule, was warm and positive.
"It was a new atmosphere," said Swedish Prime Minister Goran Persson, one of Major's sternest critics. Blair, said Persson, had "broken the ice".
The difference was that Blair has committed himself to Europe in a way Major -- hobbled by his narrow parliamentary majority and the pressure from the right-wingers in his ranks -- never could.
And Blair is the architect of Labour's biggest ever election victory.

Europe's leaders have been treading water for months waiting for Major's departure -- although never officially admitting it. But Blair is here to stay -- for five years at least and more unless the defeated Conservatives can stage an astonishing turnaround.

Blair has now articulated his vision for Europe. It must be, he explained, a "people's Europe" that makes sense to voters worried about the challenges, uncertainties and opportunities of the next century.
And as a man who convinced voters to give him a parliamentary majority of 179, Britain's biggest since 1832, Blair's claims to speak for ordinary voters is persuasive.
